items.title: Higher oil prices drive up Dutch industrial turnover
items.summary: Dutch industrial turnover rose 8.4% in the second quarter, the biggest year-on-year rise since the end of 2022. But it...
items.body_text:
Higher oil prices drive up Dutch industrial turnover
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch industrial turnover rose 8.4% in the second quarter, the biggest year-on-year rise since the end of 2022. But it was driven mainly by higher oil prices rather than a real recovery, figures from national statistics agency CBS show.
Prices across industry were 5% higher than a year ago, so more than half of the rise reflects costlier goods rather than higher sales. Last year, turnover had fallen 0.7%.
The growth was also uneven, with refineries and the chemical industry taking in 31.2% more than a year earlier, and the oil industry alone up 83% as its selling prices rose 40.5%.
The higher oil prices stem from disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been largely shut since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. With few ships getting through, prices have risen – the same reason petrol has been so expensive in the Netherlands this year.
Not every sector grew. Food, drink and tobacco fell furthest, with turnover down 6.7%, mainly because selling prices dropped. Shoppers are unlikely to see that in the supermarket yet, as there are many steps between factory and shelf.
Manufacturers are more optimistic about the months ahead, with more expecting higher turnover than at any point since mid-2022. Even so, many still cannot find enough workers, and slightly more industrial companies went bankrupt than a year earlier, CBS said.

items.title: “Exceptional” 17th-century sketchbook donated to Rijksmuseum
items.summary: A 17th-century sketchbook containing 30 drawings has been hailed as a rare find after it was donated to the Rijksmuseum...
items.body_text:
“Exceptional” 17th-century sketchbook donated to Rijksmuseum
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A 17th-century sketchbook containing 30 drawings has been hailed as a rare find after it was donated to the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.
Several of the sketches have been attributed to the Frisian painter Rombould Uylenburgh, who was a well-known artist in his day but fell into obscurity following his death in 1627 or 1628.
The book is known as the Van Eeghen sketchbook, after the family of Amsterdam merchants who owned it for three centuries. The sketches, some of which were made on blue paper, have retained their colour because the book has not been on display.
The Rijksmuseum said it was unusual for an artist’s sketchbook from the 17th century to survive intact for so long. More commonly, the drawings are torn out and sold individually, or lost.
Only two sketches and a handful of paintings by Uylenburgh were thought to have survived when the sketchbook resurfaced in 1935.
The drawings in the book were only attributed to him in 2013, after the owner saw they were similar to one of the artist’s works in the Rijksmuseum’s collection.
Uylenburgh was born in Friesland in 1580 but spent most of his life in Poland after his family emigrated to Krakow. He because the court painter of King Sigismund III Vasa and went on to build a successful career in the port city of Danzig.
His brother, Hendrik, returned to the Dutch Republic and based himself in Amsterdam. By 1625 had established himself as Rembrandt’s main art dealer and is believed to have introduced the painter to his cousin, Saskia van Uylenburgh, who married Rembrandt in 1633.
The Van Eeghen sketchbook is the focus of a display in the museum from August 19 until November 29.

items.title: Poland “99% sure” fugitive opposition politician is in pro-Russian breakaway region of Moldova
items.summary: Marcin Romanowski's whereabouts have been unknown since he fled Hungary, where he previously held asylum.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, says that they are “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia.
Last week, judicial authorities in Poland confirmed that they had received a letter purportedly from Romanowski, who is wanted in Poland for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
In the document, Romanowski claimed to be in Transnistria and requested safe passage back to Poland. However, as the authenticity of the letter had not been confirmed, some media outlets speculated that the politician may not, in fact, be in Transnistria.
Meanwhile, the Moldovan authorities quickly announced that they had no record of Romanowski travelling to Transnistria, which is a landlocked territory that only has borders with Moldova and Ukraine and operates no commercial passenger flights.
A former government minister who fled criminal charges in Poland appears to be in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia.
Marcin Romanowski's whereabouts have been unknown since he left Hungary earlier this year https://t.co/MPWroFVbMe
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 13, 2026
Speaking on Tuesday morning, Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, said they have “still not confirmed” the veracity of Romanowski’s claim to be in Transnistria, reported broadcaster RMF.
However, shortly afterwards, speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said he wanted to address the issue given there has been “a great deal of speculation and misinformation regarding Mr Romanowski and his whereabouts”.
“I can say that the intelligence services of other countries in the region with which we cooperate have confirmed to us the information that Mr Romanowski is 99% certain – I say that just in case – to be in Transnistria, in Tiraspol,” he continued, referring to the capital of the breakaway region.
"Pan Romanowski znajduje się na 99 procent w Naddniestrzu. Chyba nie trzeba tu komentarzy"
Donald Tusk podczas posiedzenia rządu ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/muVQVKrOTs
— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 18, 2026
Transnistria is a narrow strip of land in eastern Moldova that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s as the Soviet Union collapsed, fighting a war between 1990 and 1992.
Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Its flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle.
Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. Various experts and former intelligence officials have noted that it would be impossible for Romanowski to enter without Russia’s approval.
The fact that Romanowski appears to be hiding there has led to criticism of PiS, the party Romanowski still technically serves as an MP and which publicly takes a strongly anti-Russian position.
“If it is true that [Romanowski] is in Transnistria, a republic not recognised by anyone, de facto controlled 100% by Russia, then it must have happened through and with the participation of Russia,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last week.
“Escaping under the Russian umbrella is the worst possible thing, because not only are they cowardly, but they are also joining the enemy of Poland,” he added.

items.title: FedEx-led €7.8bn takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost wins EU approval
items.summary: InPost has expanded rapidly in recent years through its pioneering use of parcel lockers.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The European Commission has granted approval for a consortium led by American transportation conglomerate FedEx to take over Polish delivery giant InPost in a deal worth €7.8 billion (33.7 billion zloty).
InPost, which operates in France, Spain, the UK, Portugal, Italy and the Benelux countries, as well as in its home market, confirmed on Tuesday that it had received the green light from the EU for the deal, which was announced in February.
If it goes through, the takeover will see a consortium made up of FedEx along with existing InPost investors, Advent, A&R, and PPF, purchase all of the company’s shares at a price of €15.60 each.
Konsorcjum inwestorów, w którym jednym z uczestników jest amerykański @FedEx, uzyskało bezwarunkową zgodę KE na nabycie wszystkich akcji @InPostPL @RBrzoska https://t.co/F4AleTCViO
— WNP.PL (@wnppl) August 18, 2026
The group behind the deal says the aim is to help InPost continue its recent rapid expansion. The firm will retain its name, branding and Polish headquarters. Founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska will remain in place, as well as being a major shareholder through A&R, which is his investment vehicle.
The deal will see Advent, an American private equity firm, and FedEx each hold 37% of InPost. A&R would have 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. Currently, PPF holds 28.75%, A&R 12.49%, and Advent 6.5%.
The initial offer period for the consortium’s takeover was due to end on 27 July. However, on 22 July, it was extended until 18 September due to the fact that antitrust proceedings in the EU and Vietnam were still ongoing.
In its announcement today of EU approval, InPost noted that it is still awaiting a green light from the Vietnam Competition Commission but expects a decision to be made by 8 September. Although the Polish company has no operations in Vietnam, FedEx has been present on the market since 1994.
InPost has grown rapidly in recent years through its pioneering use of parcel lockers, first in Poland and then across western Europe. In the UK, it has established a network of over 14,000 parcel lockers, including in branches of the British Post Office.
In June this year, French President Emannuel Macron thanked InPost for its latest investment in France, where the firm – which operates there through its subsidiary Mondial Relay – is planning to spend a further €500 million to expand its presence.
In the first quarter of 2026, InPost saw its revenue rise 31% year-on-year to reach 3.9 billion zloty. That included 121% growth in the UK, 28% in the Eurozone and 9% in Poland itself.
However, the group’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA), a measure of profitability of business operations, were down 4% to 902 million zloty.

items.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
items.summary: The bus was carrying Catholic pilgrims back to Poland.
items.body_text:

Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep.
Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected.
BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3
📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw
— Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026
The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured.
According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News.
Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”.
Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims.
I am grateful to all those who took part…
— Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026
Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there.
Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary.
Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation.
Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”.
The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash.

items.title: Presidential candidate Ülle Madise: Estonia must look to its own interests
items.summary: Estonia must look after its own interests and do what benefits the country while remaining a valuable partner to its allies, presidential candidate Ülle Madise tells ERR in an interview.
items.body_text:
Presidential candidate Ülle Madise: Estonia must look to its own interests
Estonia must look after its own interests and do what benefits the country while remaining a valuable partner to its allies, presidential candidate Ülle Madise tells ERR in an interview.
In a previous interview with ERR, you emphasized that you are willing to run for president provided you can maintain an image of impartiality and are not associated with any one party, the coalition or the opposition. Does it damage your image of impartiality if you ultimately fail to receive endorsement signatures from much of the conservative camp?
I don't believe it does. I don't think people's worldviews can be divided so rigidly into two groups, with some being conservatives and others liberals. When I spoke about ideological camps, I had a somewhat more complex picture in mind.
The Social Democrats, who are currently in opposition, were the first to put my name forward as a possible candidate. I believe the Social Democrats' economic and social policy views differ considerably from those represented by the Reform Party and Eesti 200. It is entirely natural for all the parties represented in the Riigikogu to represent a range of different interests and views — that is exactly as it should be.
My point was that I have served as an impartial chancellor of justice and have always remained impartial. I have never become a passionate advocate for any particular cause, no matter how strong the pressure has been, even under very difficult circumstances. The chancellor of justice must be credible and trustworthy in the eyes of everyone in Estonia, regardless of their worldview.
Under the Constitution, exactly the same applies to the president. That is why I want to maintain my image of impartiality as well. From a political-strategy standpoint, there is always a desire either to criticize or praise people in such positions, but neither the criticism nor the praise is necessarily sincere.
Center Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart told "Aktuaalne kaamera" news on Monday that you will not receive support across political camps. There will be two candidates and two camps. At your meeting yesterday, did Kõlvart explain why he has concluded that you will not receive cross-camp support?
We don't know that, because the deadline for nominating candidates is August 24. That is how it should be in a parliamentary system. Over the years, people may have been given a misleading impression of the president's role and the presidential election process. August 24 is when candidates are nominated. What matters to me is that I am not associated with any one party, the coalition or the opposition. It is already clear that this will not be the case.
Following my meetings on Monday and Tuesday, I can say that the questions from members of the Riigikogu were very good and the discussions were interesting. I did not sense any disagreements in my meetings with Isamaa, the Center Party or unaffiliated MPs. I said the same things I have said all along, things that I believe are appropriate for a president whose role is to advance Estonia's future and inspire its people.
The questions varied, but I answered them from the same set of values and views. I thought we connected very well. Whatever decisions members of the Riigikogu make are theirs to make freely. I cannot say whether, in these difficult circumstances, they will seek an independent and balanced mediator — the "mortar" in the walls of the Estonian state, so to speak — who can maintain balance and represent Estonia abroad without exposing its domestic problems, while at the same time ensuring that Estonia is noticed and recognized as a country worth defending.
I cannot say how an agreement will be reached in the Riigikogu, what considerations will factor into it or how much attention will be paid to the Riigikogu elections and political maneuvering. That is for members of the Riigikogu to decide. I can thank all the MPs for their good questions

items.title: Forest report warns Estonia is cutting trees faster than they can regrow
items.summary: A forest inventory published by the Estonian Environment Agency shows that Estonia's forests are not recovering fast enough. The sector also lacks consensus on how much forest should be protected and how much should be harvested.
items.body_text:
Forest report warns Estonia is cutting trees faster than they can regrow
A forest inventory published by the Estonian Environment Agency shows that Estonia's forests are not recovering fast enough. The sector also lacks consensus on how much forest should be protected and how much should be harvested.
According to the 2026 statistical forest inventory, Estonia's forest area has increased slightly and forest reserves have stabilized. Environment Agency director Taimar Ala noted, however, that forests are being cut faster than they can grow back.
"In managed forests, harvest volumes have exceeded net growth for about seven to eight years. The more we cut today, the sooner the moment arrives when harvest volumes will fall," Ala said.
Ala said species‑rich forests are increasing, but pines and spruces are declining because clear‑cut conifer areas usually grow back as deciduous forests. Conifer forests therefore require especially careful management.
"When money has been taken out of the forest, some of it must be put back. Forest management activities are very necessary here," Ala said.
Hardo Becker, head of forestry at the Estonian Forest and Wood Industries Association, does not see the timber industry as responsible for the decline in spruces and pines. He blames unfavorable weather and pests.
"The fact that species composition varies to some extent — whether due to a forest owner's decisions or climate change — is actually quite expected for the wood industry. We should focus more on growing more cubic meters per hectare in the future," Becker said.
Estonian Fund for Nature forest expert Eliisa Pass said conifers have decreased because of excessive logging.
"The government should work to reduce harvest volumes, and that requires changing various logging rules in our laws. For example, tree felling ages should be raised, especially for conifers, which have been heavily overcut," Pass said.
Becker does not consider reducing harvest volumes necessary. He said the real limitation for the timber industry is that non‑managed forest makes up one‑fifth of Estonia's forest land — the third‑highest share in Europe.
"When a large amount of wood has been taken out of use and placed under protection in Estonia, that has been a government decision," Becker said.
Ala said that although no major changes have occurred compared with previous years, increasing harvest volumes would not be sustainable.
"There is no overnight disappearance of opportunities, but it is clear that it is not wise to live at the expense of the future," Ala said.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Argo Ideon

items.title: Madise becomes clear front‑runner after Isamaa endorsement
items.summary: Isamaa's support for Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise in the presidential election means she has become the clear front‑runner. Even if some votes slip away in the secret ballot, four parties together have enough votes to elect the president in the Riigikogu's first round on September 2.
items.body_text:
Madise becomes clear front‑runner after Isamaa endorsement
Isamaa's support for Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise in the presidential election means she has become the clear front‑runner. Even if some votes slip away in the secret ballot, four parties together have enough votes to elect the president in the Riigikogu's first round on September 2.
Last Thursday, 62 members of the Riigikogu signed in support of nominating Madise. The signatures came from the governing Reform Party and Estonia 200, as well as the opposition Social Democratic Party.
On Tuesday, Reform Party member Mart Võrklaev, who had initially hesitated, said meetings with Madise convinced him to support her both in nomination and in the September 2 vote. That gave Madise 63 expected votes. She still needed five more to reach the required threshold.
On Tuesday evening, after several hours of discussion, Isamaa announced it would also support Madise in the presidential election. Isamaa's parliamentary group has eight members, and three additional MPs have joined the party, giving it a total of 11 votes.
Simple math shows Madise should therefore have 74 votes. Electing the president requires at least 68 votes. Isamaa politician Kalle Muuli declared triumphantly on social media that "it is Isamaa that will choose Estonia's next president, because it depends on Isamaa whether Madise gets at least 68 votes in the presidential election."
It is also possible that some unaffiliated MPs (Tõnis Mölder, Kersti Sarapuu, Enn Eesmaa), who are not tied to any party and have not clearly expressed a preference, may support Madise. Social Democrat Züleyxa Izmailova has not announced her final decision either. She told ERR on Tuesday evening that she would not sign for nominating Madise or any other candidate. How she will vote on September 2 is unknown. It is also unclear how the so‑called window‑seat MPs (especially Kalev Stoicescu), who wanted to support Tiit Land but may not be able to nominate him if he fails to gather the required 21 signatures, will vote. Madise could pick up one or two votes from that group as well.
At the same time, it must be remembered that the vote is secret, and signatures on nomination papers are not binding commitments. As Võrklaev said on Tuesday: "In the end, each member of the Riigikogu chooses the president individually, according to their conscience, in a secret ballot — not one or another parliamentary group."
Madise's supporters still wondered on Tuesday whether the Reform Party's own votes would hold. Some pointed out that more MPs might leave the party in the fall, especially to join Isamaa, which could reduce Madise's support in the secret ballot. That concern arose when Isamaa had not yet decided whether to support Madise or Land. Now that Isamaa has announced its support for Madise, that fear is much smaller.
But even Isamaa's own votes cannot be taken for granted. Before the party's decision, Isamaa politician Riina Solman said the party's votes were split evenly between Madise and Land. The hours‑long discussion confirmed that reaching a unified position was not easy. And it is worth remembering that the September 2 vote is secret.
For historical context, here are the vote totals presidents have received when elected in the Riigikogu:
1992 – Lennart Meri 59 votes. At the time, if no candidate received more than half of the votes cast in the popular vote, the Riigikogu elected the president. Meri received 59 votes and Arnold Rüütel 31, and 59 was enough under the law then in force.
Since 1996, the current presidential election procedure has applied. In 1996, 2001 and 2006, the Riigikogu failed to elect a president, and the choice was made by the electoral college composed of Riigikogu members and representatives of local councils.
2011 – Toomas Hendrik Ilves 73 votes. Ilves and Indrek Tarand faced off in the Riigikogu. Ilves received 73 votes and Tarand 25, and Ilves was re‑elected.
2016 – Kersti Kaljulaid 81 votes. No candidate receiv

items.title: ‘Terror-Free Turkey’ Process Could Boost Ankara’s International Status
items.summary: An end to the decades-long conflict between Turkey and the Kurdish militants of the PKK could transform Turkey’s geopolitical and economic relationships with its neighbours and Euro-Atlantic allies.
items.body_text:
Turkey’s attempt to bring four decades of conflict with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) to an end is usually discussed primarily as a domestic political question. Understandably, the process named by Ankara as “Terror-Free Turkey” is framed around internal security, disarmament and the future relationship between the Turkish state and its Kurdish citizens. Yet such a reading is incomplete.
The conflict with the PKK has never been merely an internal security challenge. For decades, it has shaped Turkey’s relations with Iraq and Syria, complicated its dealings with Washington and European governments and absorbed substantial military and intelligence resources.
The Turkish parliament’s adoption of the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration on August 10 must therefore also be understood as a development with potentially significant foreign policy consequences. Turkey will not automatically become more powerful if the process succeeds, but it could gain greater freedom to redistribute political, military and diplomatic attention across several theatres.
The central question is whether Ankara can convert a reduction in one of its longest running security burdens into greater regional room for manoeuvre. Foreign policy influence is never generated automatically by the disappearance of a single security problem. What remains decisive are economic resources, institutional quality, diplomatic credibility, military capabilities, alliance structures and the behaviour of other states.

items.title: Serbian Economy Braces for Ripple Effect of Danube Cargo Slowdown
items.summary: The hit to cargo transport from a dramatic drop in Danube water levels will be felt across the Serbian economy for months to come, experts warn.
items.body_text:
Severe drought has slowed cargo transport on the Serbian stretch of the Danube almost to a halt, impacting supply chains and likely driving up prices.
In July, Elixir Group, operator of one of the country’s main Danube ports, Prahovo, reported an increase of roughly 31 per cent year-on-year in the amount of cargo it handled. That all changed towards the end of the month, when the water level at Prahovo fell 45 centimetres between July 17 and August 18, forcing barge operators to drastically reduce the loads they carry.
“Due to conditions on the lower Danube, navigation has been completely suspended, directly preventing cargo vessels from reaching the Port of Prahovo,” said Dragan Stevovic, Elixir’s director of logistics and distribution, chemical division.

items.title: Russian Propaganda Thrives in Greek Media Via ‘Disinformation Laundering’
items.summary: Despite a ban on Russian media outlets in Greece in line with EU sanctions, pro-Kremlin content often finds its way into the country’s news as fringe claims are ‘laundered’ into mainstream outlets.
items.body_text:
A report splashed across Greek online media last month declared sensationally that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s parents were being investigated for corruption, after $11 million dollars was found in their bank accounts.
It wasn’t true and was debunked by Ellinika Hoaxes, a Greek fact-checking organisation. Yet the story wasn’t just published by fringe pro-Russian sites such as Pronews. It was also published by Newsbomb, a highly popular Greek-language site belonging to the DPG Digital Media Group. DPG is owned by Dimitris Giannakopoulos, a businessman and the owner of Panathinaikos football club, who is sympathetic to Vladimir Putin.
Some of the reports were accompanied by a video taken from a Russia-friendly X account which purported to be from Europe Today, a show from French pan-European TV news network, Euronews. But as Ellinika Hoaxes pointed out, the Euronews logo in the video is different from the regular one, which has a blue background and white letters and not a white background with blue letters.
In its debunking, Ellinika Hoaxes pointed out that the made-up Zelensky story was “yet another case of fabricated fake news” originating from a Russian disinformation network, Matryoshka. Also known as Operation Overload, Matryoshka is a coordinated Russian propaganda network that creates and spreads fake news and videos, deepfakes and memes using logos of well-known Western media outlets.

items.body_text:
Turnout did not exceed 25 percent in any of the municipalities. Continue reading
Following its election defeat this spring, FIDESZ launched a comprehensive investigation to examine the party’s entire organizational, structural, and personnel situation, Magyar Nemzet reported. Based on a detailed internal questionnaire with more than 30 questions, party headquarters aims this time not only to identify the technical mistakes made during the election campaign but also to find out what underlying causes, in the members’ view, led to the failure.
The tone of the questions is unusually blunt in several respects. Members are asked to comment on whether FIDESZ has become detached from everyday reality and the problems people face, and to what extent dissatisfaction stemming from economic difficulties contributed to the defeat.
The questionnaire lists the erosion of the party’s moral credibility as a separate option, citing several specific cases.
The survey also asks whether FIDESZ ran an overly negative campaign or whether voters simply did not believe the party’s messages.
One of the most interesting sections of the questionnaire deals with the future of FIDESZ. Members are asked to state their views on whether it would be sufficient to continue the current policies with the existing leadership, whether minor changes and adjustments are necessary, or whether a complete overhaul and rejuvenation of the party should be undertaken.
Far more radical scenarios are also being considered. Respondents are also asked to comment on whether, in addition to FIDESZ, a new, movement-style right-wing community should be organized; furthermore, it is suggested that
FIDESZ should, if necessary, be dissolved and a new right-wing, conservative party founded with new members.
A separate section deals with the party’s communication. It indicates that the party leadership is interested in providing internal information to its members. The party is also examining the sources from which its own members obtain information. This is not a minor issue, as following the election defeat, one of the most important questions for FIDESZ could be how it can more effectively reach and mobilize its own supporters in the coming period.
The questionnaire also asks respondents to separately evaluate the suitability of several leading FIDESZ politicians. Among the questions is whether FIDESZ should stand by all its leaders and elected officials, regardless of the allegations made against them. However, members can also send a direct message to Viktor Orbán: At the end of the questionnaire, they can use a separate text field to write what they would like to say to the party chairman.
Through a series of questions, the questionnaire also examines FIDESZ’s political strategy regarding the TISZA Party. Respondents are asked to state their views on whether Péter Magyar and the TISZA are establishing an authoritarian system and whether FIDESZ should pursue a policy of resistance rather than simply act as an opposition party.
The questions indicate that the party leadership is already gathering internal opinions in order to develop its strategy for the next political term.
In parallel with the survey, former Minister of Construction and Transportation János Lázár is assessing the state of the party organization during his tour of the country. The party executive committee tasked the politician with examining FIDESZ’s entire nationwide infrastructure, the state of the organizations in rural areas, the operations of the offices, and the question of whom the party can count on in the coming period.
According to Bertalan Havasi, FIDESZ’s communications director, the goal is to have a clear picture by the start of the autumn political season of the party’s organizational, structural, and personnel status, as well as who the party can count on.
Via Magyar Nemzet; Featured photo: MTI/Miniszterelnöki Kommunikációs Főosztály/Kaiser Ákos

Csaba Németh wrote that two of the injured patients are being treated in serious, life-threatening but stable condition in the Central Anesthesiology and Intensive Care Unit (KAITO).

items.title: Debrecen Flower Carnival to Bring Floral Floats and International Performers to the City
items.summary: The Holy Crown flower float at the Debrecen Flower Carnival on August 20, 2025 The Debrecen Flower Carnival will offer visitors with 350 events between August 18 and 23. On the main day of the event, August 20, 12 flower-decorated floats will parade through the city, accompanied by 17 Hungarian artistic groups and nine international […] The post Debrecen Flower Carnival to Bring Floral Floats and International Performers to the City appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
An estimated 300,000 people visited Debrecen for the celebrations on August 20, including the carnival itself.Continue reading
The Debrecen Flower Carnival will offer visitors with 350 events between August 18 and 23. On the main day of the event, August 20, 12 flower-decorated floats will parade through the city, accompanied by 17 Hungarian artistic groups and nine international troupes, Magyar Nemzet reported.
The Debrecen Flower Carnival looks back on a tradition spanning more than a century: the first such event was held in 1905, and the Flower Carnival was organized for the first time in 1966. László Papp (Fidesz-KDNP), mayor of Debrecen (eastern Hungary), said at a press conference on Monday that the event had since become one of the city’s symbols and is closely linked to the celebration of the founding of the Hungarian state.
On August 20, 12 flower floats will parade through the streets. The parade will be accompanied by 17 Hungarian artistic groups as well as nine international troupes, with performers coming from France, Mexico, Italy, Belgium, Germany, Serbia, South Korea, and China.
This year, CATL Debrecen will delight visitors of the Debrecen Flower Carnival with its most spectacular flower float to date. The company is taking part in one of the city’s most important community events for the third time,
bringing to life the legendary Hungarian horse, Kincsem, and the symbolism of the Chinese Fire Horse through a unique composition featuring moving elements and a light installation.
For CATL Debrecen, it is important to play an active role in the community life of Debrecen and to support landmark events that have brought the local community together for many years. In addition to the Campus Festival,
the company has been the main sponsor of the Debrecen Flower Carnival for the third consecutive year.
On August 20, CATL Debrecen will present a distinctive composition to the public that reflects both Chinese and Hungarian cultural elements.
At the heart of this year’s float stands Kincsem, the most successful undefeated Hungarian racehorse in history, who achieved victory in 54 races between 1876 and 1879. The monumental, three-dimensional sculpture of Kincsem symbolizes perseverance, excellence, and determination. Alongside Kincsem, stylized Fire Horses will appear.
According to Chinese tradition,
2026 is the Year of the Fire Horse, symbolizing energy, courage, progress, and forward-looking thinking.
There will be no shortage of concerts during Carnival Week: several free large-scale concerts will be held at Kossuth Square, and Valmar will perform on August 20.
Via Magyar Nemzet, Press Release; Featured photo: MTI/Oláh Tamás

items.title: Valter Attila újra indul a spanyol háromhetes kerékpáros körversenyen
items.summary: A 28 éves magyar bringás is ott van a Bahrain Victorious nyolcfős keretében.
items.body_text:
Valter Attila újra indul a spanyol háromhetes kerékpáros körversenyen
Valter Attila is indul a szombaton rajtoló Vuelta a España országúti kerékpáros körversenyen. A Bahrain Victorious csapat szerdán jelentette be a versenyen induló nyolcfős keretét, köztük a 28 éves magyar kerékpárost – írta az MTI. A nagyobb nevek közül a baszk Pello Bilbao és a kolumbiai Santiago Buitrago is ott lesz a Bahrain Victorious csapatában.
Az idei Vuelta augusztus 22-én rajtol el egy monacói egyenkénti időfutammal, az utolsó szakasz pedig szeptember 13-án lesz Granadában. A verseny legnagyobb esélyese az ötszörös Tour de France-győztes Tadej Pogačar lesz, aki korábban még nem nyert Vueltát.
Valter pályafutása hetedik Grand Tourjára készül, korábban négy Giro d'Italián és két Vueltán szerepelt. A 2021-es olasz körversenyen három napig viselte az összetett első helyezettjének járó rózsaszín trikót. 2020-ban megnyerte az összetettet a Tour de Hongrie-n, a 2024-es párizsi olimpia országúti mezőnyversenyén pedig negyedik lett. Mezőnyversenyben háromszoros, időfutamban kétszeres magyar bajnok országúton.
Valter a 2023-as Vueltán – még a Jumbo-Visma versenyzőjeként – 22. lett az összetettben, egy évvel később pedig a 25. helyen fejezte be a spanyol körversenyt. A 2024-es Vuelta volt Valter legutóbbi háromhetese, azóta nem szerepelt magyar kerékpáros a legnagyobb körversenyeken.

items.summary: A rendőrség már keresi a gyanúsítottat, aki a múlt héten legalább hat emberre rontott rá az uctán.
items.body_text:
Ijesztő babamaszkban fenyegeti a járókelőket valaki Philadelphiában
Ijesztő babamaszkban ijesztgeti és fenyegeti a járókelőket egy férfi Philadelphiában – írja a BBC. A rendőrség már keresi a gyanúsítottat, aki a múlt héten legalább hat emberre rontott rá a városháza környékén.
A térfigyelő kamerák alapján a férfi reggelente csap le. Az egyik áldozatát kergetni kezdte, miközben azt kérdezte tőle, „készen áll-e a halálra”. A nő megbotlott és megsérült, a támadó pedig a metróba menekült.
Egy másik futót azzal zaklatott, hogy ki tud gyorsabban futni, majd reakció híján továbbállt. Az áldozatok szerint az egész olyan volt, mint valami beteg játék.
A rendőrség fotókat és videót is közzétett a férfiról, aki a szemtanúk szerint vakus telefonnal rögzíti a támadásokat.
Egyelőre nem tudni, hogy egy értelmetlen közösségimédia-kihívásról van-e szó, esetleg utcai átverésről (prankről), de a gyanúsított ellen zaklatás, fenyegetőzés és testi sértés miatt indult eljárás.

items.title: Trump órákkal az életbelépés előtt halasztotta el a Kanadára kivetett vám bevezetését
items.summary: Az amerikai elnök szerint sikerült megegyeznie a két országnak.
items.body_text:
Trump órákkal az életbelépés előtt halasztotta el a Kanadára kivetett vám bevezetését
Három nap erejéig elhalasztotta a Kanadára kivetett 50 százalékos vám életbe léptetését Donald Trump, írja a CNN. Az amerikai elnök szerint Kanada és az Egyesült Államok megállapodást kötött, és már a dokumentumokat véglegesítik, így felfüggeszti az 50 százalékos kereskedelmi vámok bevezetését. A vámok szerda reggel léptek volna hatályba, Trump órákkal előtte tett bejelentést a közösségi oldalán.
Az amerikai elnök bejelentését egyébként többnapnyi egyeztetés előzte meg. Mark Carney kanadai miniszterelnök és Trump hétfőn beszéltek egymással, és kedden is folytatódtak a tárgyalások. A kanadai kormányfő is megerősítette, hogy a vámokat felfüggesztették, augusztus 21-ig. Szerinte noha sikerült jelentős eredményt elérni az egyeztetésekkel, még mindig sok a tennivaló, mondta Carney.
A korábban bejelentett vámok számos kanadai termék importjára vonatkoztak volna, többek között tejtermékekre, alkoholos italokra és bútorokra is. Kína mellett Kanada volt a másik olyan ország, aki nem hagyta volna annyiban Trump vámjait, és válaszként kész lett volna hasonló vámokat kivetni az Egyesült Államokra – ám Carney végül nem hozott ilyen döntést.
A vámok miatti feszültség Kínával inkább fokozódott az elmúlt hetekben. A két ország már több vámot és szankciót bejelentett egymás termékeire, főleg a drónokra és más techipari termékekre vonatkozóan.

items.body_text:
Prague's Groovy Market Fest Returns After a Successful Debut
Prague Morning
A new urban festival is aiming to become a regular fixture on Prague’s cultural calendar after attracting 1,200 visitors to its first edition in Riegrovy sady.
Groovy Market Fest, held on August 1, brought together food, design, music and local brands in a format inspired by European city markets.
According to the organizers, around 85% of visitors were tourists or foreign residents of Prague, highlighting the event’s appeal beyond the Czech-speaking audience.
The festival will return to Riegrovy sady on September 5, with further editions planned for October, November and December.
From Barcelona to Prague
Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food culture.
Their interest in international gastronomy also led them to compete in Spain. In 2025, they won first place in the Cooking The Street competition, where their dish was judged by a professional panel that included chefs Beñat Ormaetxea and Jon Kepa Aurrecoetxea.
After returning to Prague, they decided to develop their own event, drawing inspiration from markets such as Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market.
The First Edition
Food Garden focused on gastronomy, while Palm Street featured local products and handmade goods. The Design Zone presented Czech brands working in fashion, design and art.
Rather than filling the site with as many vendors as possible, the organizers selected a smaller number of participants. They say the approach was intended to create a more coherent experience for visitors.
Music was another part of the programme, with live performances and DJ sets throughout the event. Visitors could also attend a masterclass focused on preparing the festival’s signature Groovy cocktail.
Additional editions are scheduled for October 3, November 7 and December 5, all at the same location.
Tickets for upcoming editions are available through GoOut.

items.body_text:
Faster Than the Metro. New Bus is Now Linking Prague 8 and Prague 6
Prague Morning
A new bus service running through Prague’s Blanka tunnel has begun operating, offering a direct connection between the northern part of the city and Dejvice.
Bus line 145 connects Čimice and Kobylisy in Prague 8 with Hradčanská and Dejvická in Prague 6. The journey takes around 15 minutes, according to Prague’s public transport authority ROPID.
The same trip by metro requires a change between lines C and A in the city centre and takes around 22 minutes.
Including the time spent walking through stations and using escalators, the journey can take about half an hour.
The first day of operation brought mostly positive results, with many buses arriving on time or even ahead of schedule. The real test will come during regular weekday traffic, when congestion around Prague is heavier.
Where the new bus runs
In the direction from Čimice to Dejvice, line 145 serves:
Sídliště Čimice – Čimice – Libeňská – Řepínská – Podhajská pole – Čimický háj – Písečná – Služská – Kobylisy – Okrouhlická – Vychovatelna – Hradčanská – Vítězné náměstí – Dejvická
The return route follows the same corridor in the opposite direction.
The key feature of line 145 is its use of the Blanka tunnel, allowing buses to avoid the city centre and provide a direct connection between Prague 8 and Prague 6.
The new route is expected to make commuting easier for residents of Čimice, Kobylisy and surrounding neighbourhoods, while providing an alternative to the metro for journeys towards Dejvice and Hradčanská.

items.body_text:
Leo Express to Launch Direct Prague-Brno Trains in December
Prague Morning
Leo Express is set to begin operating direct trains between Prague and Brno in December, marking the private carrier’s first direct connection between the two cities.
The company has already been serving passengers in the South Moravian Region, but its trains have so far bypassed Brno.
Over the past year, travellers from towns such as Hodonín and Břeclav have been able to use Leo Express services to reach Prague, travelling via Přerov and Olomouc.
The new Prague–Brno service will change that, putting the carrier directly on one of the Czech Republic’s busiest rail routes.
There is, however, one limitation for passengers travelling to Prague.
Leo Express trains do not serve Prague Main Station. In Prague, passengers must use Praha-Libeň station, which may be less convenient for those travelling to the city centre.
Leo Express was founded by businessman Leoš Novotný and has operated passenger trains in the Czech Republic since 2012.
The company has gradually expanded its network in the Czech Republic and abroad, competing with established operators such as České dráhy and RegioJet.
The Prague–Brno connection is expected to become another important part of the company’s Czech network from December.

Garibashvili Alleges Attempts at His ‘Political Destruction,’ Announces ‘Fight’ in Widely Anticipated Statement
In a widely anticipated statement published on August 18, jailed former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili alleged that the “anti-corruption battle” launched last year sought his “political destruction,” noting Mamuka Mdinaradze was the one who sent him a “letter” about confessing to a corruption case. Garibashvili announced his intention to fight.
The statement came a day after his previous post, where the ex-PM shared a fragment of a “letter” he said was sent to him “on [Bidzina] Ivanishvili’s instruction.” The letter, with the author unknown, warned of forthcoming corruption charges, offering as one option that “we confess” to one of such cases, with the confession intended to spare him additional prison years but also to serve as a guarantee that Garibashvili would not consider returning to politics after his release from prison.
In the August 17 post, Garibashvili also pledged to reveal his “truth” the next day, and said Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream government bear responsibility for his and his family’s safety.
In the August 18 statement, Garibashvili says that the alleged letter was sent to him in July by Mamuka Mdinaradze, the current Regional Development Minister who till late July served as State Minister for Coordination of Law Enforcement Bodies.
The new statement does not explicitly mention Bidzina Ivanishvili, the ruling Georgian Dream party’s billionaire founder and honorary chairman, but refers to “a person dear to me.” Garibashvili also does not explicitly name the group or persons who have been seeking his “political destruction.”
August 18 Statement
In the four-paragraph statement, Garibashvili writes:
“I want to tell the public the truth on why I am in prison. The main goal of the so-called ‘fight against corruption’ campaign launched last year was my imprisonment and political destruction. I state with full responsibility that I did everything I could to avoid entering into a confrontation with the team and with a person dear to me. Precisely with this goal, I refused to engage in a legal battle and followed through with a process that was destructive for me, so as not to harm the interests of the state and the team.”
He then argues that, in turn, he was only subjected to “staged dirty provocation, many lies and injustice,” adding that the public “did not hear a single word” from him through all this time and that he “endured this ordeal with complete patience.”
“But unexpectedly to me, in July, I received the letter I published yesterday, which was sent to me by Mamuka Mdinaradze. That same day, I made my position clear to him, reiterating that I had no intention of returning to politics, and, in order to address the aforementioned ‘risk,’ I offered him my own vision,” the statement reads. “In response, however, I was told by them that there remained a 1 percent risk that I might return to politics, and that, for that, it was necessary to bring a corruption charge against me and for me to confess to it.”
According to Garibashvili, this was “the red line” which pushed him to “take the most difficult step” in his life. “Accordingly, as I have no other choice, they force me to start fighting…” he concludes.
Money Laundering Case
Garibashvili currently serves a five-year sentence following a plea deal in a money laundering case, which came amid a series of prosecutions and a declared anti-corruption drive by Georgian Dream targeting former officials and business associates linked to the ruling party. One of Ivanishvili’s closest aides prior to coming to politics, he served as Georgian prime minister twice, from 2013 to 2015 and again from 2021 to 2024.

items.body_text:
Georgia Among Over 40 Countries Flagged in White House Report Over Risk of Illegal Transshipment of Chinese Goods
Georgia was among more than 40 countries identified in a White House report as being associated with elevated risks of illegal transshipment of goods to the United States to evade U.S. tariffs, mainly on Chinese goods.
According to the report titled “The Great Transshipment Scam,” Chinese goods subject to high U.S. tariffs are increasingly being routed through third countries, where they may be relabeled, repackaged, minimally processed, or accompanied by altered documentation to create the appearance of a different country of origin before entering the U.S. market.
The report groups the identified jurisdictions into three categories: “Diversified Scale Leaders,” including Canada, the European Union and India; “Scale Leaders with Significant Economic Integration with China,” including Brazil, Indonesia and Turkey; and “Small, Opportunistic Chinese Targets,” the biggest tier, which includes Georgia alongside countries such as Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Morocco and Uzbekistan.
“Azerbaijan and Georgia provide rail and dry port transit, consolidation, and overland-to-maritime connections,” the report says.
Georgia is also listed in the report’s “Functional Architecture of the Shadow Transshipment Network” as an illustrative country in the Belt and Road overland nodes cluster, alongside Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, with a core role in rail and dry-port transit, consolidation, and overland-to-maritime handoff.
Asked following a briefing on August 18 to comment on Georgia’s inclusion in the report, Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze questioned whether the document was based on facts.
“Is there any specific fact there?.. I don’t think there is any specific fact…We always ask for facts, but then they cannot provide us with facts,” he said in response to a question from TV Pirveli.
When the reporter noted that the White House would presumably have based the report on facts, Kobakhidze pushed back.
“Why would it? Various sides have often written many things without facts. Therefore, do not draw such conclusions. It may write something based on facts, or it may not be based on facts…Someone may deliberately provide the White House with incorrect information,” he said.
“We are doing everything to ensure that no such scheme exists in the country. Let them provide us with facts on any issue, and we will respond accordingly,” Kobakhidze added.

items.title: Gharibashvili claims Ivanishvili pressured him to confess to crime he didn’t commit
items.summary: The imprisoned former prime minister says the letter offered him a deal to admit to corruption charges in exchange for a 5-year sentence.
items.body_text:
Georgia’s imprisoned former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili has claimed he was told to confess to a crime he did not commit or face a possible lengthy jail sentence.
On Monday, Gharibashvili and his wife, Nunuka Tamazashvili posted a photo of a fragment of a letter they said had been sent on Ivanishvili’s instructions.
In the letter, the unnamed author claims that several corruption cases were being prepared against Gharibashvili and offers what it describes as two options: contest the charges, or admit to one or more cases as part of an agreed plea deal.
The letter says the second option would involve ‘confessions’ and the signing of witness statements, and that Gharibashvili would receive no more than a five-year sentence if he agreed to this.
It also states that, after making a statement, Gharibashvili should not return to politics, adding that potential corruption charges would serve as an ‘insurance mechanism’ against him doing so.
Monday’s post promised to share the letter in full on Tuesday, but it had yet to appear as of publication.
The letter, if genuine, may shed some light on Gharibashvili’s dramatic fallout with the ruling Georgian Dream party.
‘ “Supporters’’ like Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili and campaigns organised on social networks have raised very serious doubts and severely damaged us’, the letter said.
Inashvili is the founder and one of the leaders of the Alliance of Patriots of Georgia, an ultraconservative political party, while Chubinidze is a journalist, who has a background in history.
Following the publication of the letter, Inashvili said that Gharibashvili remained her friend.
‘I never give up on friends, that is, he is still my friend today, I have never abandoned any of my friends and I will not abandon Gharibashvili either. I will expose and fight Kobakhidze personally,’ she told TV Pirveli referring to Gharibashvili’s successor, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.
Inashvili previously claimed in October 2025 that Ivanishvili believed Gharibashvili had passed on details, including his ‘financial, commercial, and political secrets’ to the US.
She also claimed that Kobakhidze had convinced Ivanishvili that information was being leaked from the State Security Service (SSG) under its former chief, Grigol Liluashvili, who is currently also imprisoned.
‘This letter was sent to me on the instructions of Bidzina Ivanishvili. I tried and did everything to avoid taking this step, unfortunately, they left me no other choice but to stand up to this dishonourable evil!’, Gharibashvili wrote.
He added that he would publish a longer statement on Tuesday and said that ‘full responsibility for mine and my family’s safety lies with Bidzina Ivanishvili and the entire government’.
Gharibashvili had yet to publish the statement as of publication.
Kobakhidze says Gharibashvili’s claims are a matter for law enforcement
Asked about the letter during a press briefing on Monday, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said he did not know what the letter referred to.
‘I know one thing, that a specific verdict has been issued. The rest is entirely the business of law enforcement agencies,’ Kobakhidze said.
He added that he did not want to comment on Gharibashvili’s claims, partly because Gharibashvili had previously held the position of prime minister.
‘It is a very problematic statement, I would say. Not problematic for us, but for himself. I will not comment further,’ Kobakhidze said.
Asked by TV Pirveli whether he had communicated with Ivanishvili after the letter was published, Kobakhidze said they had spoken on Sunday but had not discussed the matter.
‘We did not discuss this issue in essence, we had communication yesterday regarding various issues. I do not know whether it was after the publication of the letter or before. In any case, we did not discuss this issue,’ he said.

items.title: Opinion | Questioning the hidden hierarchies within Georgian society
items.summary: The central question is not whether Georgia faces a genuine cultural conflict between Tbilisi and the provinces, but who controls scarcity.
items.body_text:
Opinion | Questioning the hidden hierarchies within Georgian society
The central question is not whether Georgia faces a genuine cultural conflict between Tbilisi and the provinces, but who controls scarcity.
The murder of 28-year-old mathematics tutor Giga Avaliani — who was attacked in Tbilisi in October 2025 after being ambushed by two teenagers, one of whom struck him; he died from his injuries later that month — has become one of Georgia’s most disturbing recent criminal cases. Beyond the crime itself, however, the public reaction has exposed a social division that deserves closer attention.
Since his death, Avaliani’s mother has publicly campaigned for broader accountability, while the families of the accused, potentially including former government officials, have also found audiences ready to hear and defend their position. There is nothing improper about insisting on due process. Yet to some observers, the case has seemed to reproduce a familiar Georgian pattern: an interconnected Tbilisi social bubble capable of mobilising sympathy, contacts, visibility, and cultural authority around the people belonging to its circles (the defendants) confronting a family associated with a very different social Georgia.
Whether this interpretation of the Avaliani case is entirely fair is less important than the ease with which many Georgians recognise the distinction behind it.
Georgia often presents itself as a small country united by language, history, and national belonging. Beneath this image, however, lies a persistent hierarchy between Tbilisi and the provinces, between city and village, and between those considered legitimate urban residents and those continually reminded that they came from elsewhere. This hierarchy even has its own vocabulary: Soplelebi — villagers; Ltolvilebi — refugees; and Naghdi Kalakelebi — real city people. These are more than geographical descriptions. They can function as social classifications, locating people within an informal hierarchy of status and belonging.
The paradox is that these categories are fluid.
A villager may move to Tbilisi, obtain an education, acquire an apartment, enter a prestigious profession, and eventually raise children who consider themselves unquestionably urban. Within one or two generations, provincial origins may disappear. Conversely, displacement, poverty, political upheaval, or migration can push an urban family towards the periphery. Geography therefore becomes part of social mobility: moving to Tbilisi is often understood as moving upwards, while association with the village may imply movement downwards.
Why has this distinction become so powerful?
One explanation may lie in the historical development of Tbilisi. Under the Russian Empire, the city became a diverse administrative and commercial centre in which Armenians, Georgians, Russians, Germans, Persians, Jews, Poles, and others participated in public life. Much of rural Georgia developed differently, remaining more linguistically homogeneous and more closely associated with local traditions, kinship structures, agriculture, and the Georgian national fabric.
This raises a historical question. Was the village imagined as the repository of something nationally authentic, while the city became associated with imperial modernisation, bureaucracy, cosmopolitanism, and later Soviet power? Or is this itself a romantic interpretation?
Perhaps there was never a deep historical conflict between a nationally rooted village and a supposedly ‘Tsarist’ city. What appears to be cultural antagonism may often be something more material: competition over resources.
Universities, ministries, prestigious schools, hospitals, professional networks, cultural institutions, political influence, and capital are concentrated in Tbilisi. Those already embedded in the city therefore enjoy advantages in accessing opportunities. Culture can then provide the vocabulary through which those advantages are justified.
Accent becomes competence.

items.title: Daghestani Islamic singer Khadizha Magomedova attacked at own home by ‘stalker of 2 years’
items.summary: The 50-year-old man was arrested as he was attempting to flee.
items.body_text:
A 50-year-old man was arrested for breaking into the home of 28-year-old nasheed singer Khadizha Magomedova in Makhachkala and threatening to kill her. Sources linked to the police have said the man had been stalking her for two years.
Russia’s Investigative Committee has opened a criminal case against the unidentified man on charges of breaking into Magomedova’s and threatening to kill her. Daghestan’s Investigative Committee announced the arrest on Monday.
Magomedova told state-run agency RIA Novosti that she heard a man’s voice in her home at night. According to her, the stranger shouted, ‘Come here!’. When she came out, the man grabbed her by the arms and began threatening her.
The singer said she took the threat seriously and feared for her life and health.
Magomedova linked the incident to the fact that she had previously blocked the man’s number. She said she usually adds all unknown numbers to her blocklist.
According to Magomedova, she was rescued by police officers patrolling the area around her home. They heard her screams, ran to the house, and detained the man as he attempted to flee.
After the incident, the singer said her arms were sore and she sought medical attention.
Magomedova also said the man had been stalking her for a while. About two months ago, her driver noticed an unfamiliar man on the staircase near her home. When they turned around and drove back towards the house, the man was already gone. Magomedova said she did not know how he had found out where she lived.
Meanwhile, the SHOT Telegram channel, which has links to Russian law enforcement agencies, reported that the man had allegedly been stalking the singer for around two years. According to the channel, he told police that he had approached Magomedova because he wanted to marry her and claimed that she had repeatedly rejected him.
Magomedova herself said she had not known the man before the incident.
Khadizha Magomedova is known in Daghestan as a performer of nasheeds, Islamic religious chants. She is also a member of the Youth Parliament under the Makhachkala City Assembly. Magomedova previously worked as an aide to a local Daghestani MP.

items.summary: Sweden Democrats call on government to pardon people convicted of defamation after warning about paedophiles – and southern Sweden imposes extreme water-saving measures after pipe burst. Here's the latest news.
items.body_text:
Sweden Democrats call on government to pardon people convicted of defamation after warning about paedophiles
The far-right Sweden Democrats want the government to pardon individuals convicted of defamation after warning others about convicted paedophiles.
"We can't have it like this, it is not in keeping with the general sense of justice," Sweden Democrat leader Jimmie Åkesson said at a press conference outside Stockholm District Court, where a high-profile defamation trial of this nature begins today.
The party's justice policy spokesperson, Henrik Vinge, said that defamation law has missed the mark.
"All those people who have warned about paedophiles, about dangerous criminals, and who have been convicted of defamation for doing so should be pardoned," he says, continuing:
"If we have our way, the government will do this – it could become a reality." (TT)
Swedish vocabulary: defamation – förtal
'Avoid showering': southern Sweden imposes extreme water-saving measures after pipe burst
Residents of Malmö and several other towns in southern Sweden have been urged to urgently save water – including being asked to forgo showers and doing the dishes – after one of the main water supply pipes sprung a major water leak.
"You may notice low water pressure in the system or that the water coming out of your tap is discoloured. Please be extremely conservative with your water usage so that the reservoirs last until the leak has been repaired," said Sydvatten, the water provider in several municipalities in southern Sweden, in a statement on Wednesday morning.
The advisory applies to all of Malmö, Svedala, Burlöv, Staffanstorp and Vellinge municipalities, as well as to Dalby and Veberöd in the municipality of Lund.
People are being asked to avoid showering, doing the dishes, washing clothes, and watering plants.
Swedish vocabulary: to avoid – att undvika
New case of measles confirmed in Stockholm
Eleven cases of measles have now been confirmed across Sweden after the Urkult folk festival in Ångermanland, which ran from July 30th to August 1st. Yesterday ten cases had been reported, but another one has now been confirmed in Stockholm.
The majority are under-18s, according to the Public Health Agency.

items.title: OPINION: The EU is betraying Brexit Brits in Sweden
items.summary: Sweden has kicked out three times more Brits after Brexit than any other European country. The European Commission has failed to lift a finger to help them. If it cares at all about the free movement of people it needs to act, argues James Savage.
items.body_text:
Brexit was a traumatic experience for hundreds of thousands of British people living across Europe, as well as for Europeans living in the UK. People who had made their lives abroad thanks to the free movement of people risked having their worlds turned upside down.
When dawn rose on 24th June 2016, many wondered whether they’d be able to keep their homes, their jobs, the lives they’d build up.
They were therefore reassured by the words of the EU’s chief negotiator, Michel Barnier. He was unequivocal:
“Individuals legally residing in the UK today must remain residents after withdrawal, including in those cases when people have no documents to prove residency.
Obviously, the same goes for UK nationals in the 27.
No one should be confronted with a mountain of red tape.”
Those were his words in a keynote speech in Florence on May 5, 2017.
Nine years later, that promise has been kept by the UK and by 26 out of 27 EU countries. With just one notable exception: Sweden.
Sweden has denied residency to 4,000 people — three times more Brits than any other EU country, according to figures Sweden has supplied to the European Commission. Many of those were denied residency due to late applications, even though they had often been living legally in Sweden for decades prior to Brexit.
They include Nichola Stanlick, who has lived in Sweden since she came here as a seven-year-old in 1984. They include Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old British widow who has lived in Sweden for 21 years. They also included well-known actor Kenny Solomons, who was kicked out of the country despite having lived here since 2012.
Happily Kenny has now found his way back and has become a Swedish citizen, but not before he had suffered five years of uncertainty. The situation for others seems far more unclear.
These are the people the EU promised to protect. They have been caught up in a combination of inflexible Swedish bureaucracy and, one suspects, a Migration Agency geared up by the government’s wider deportations policy to err on the side of kicking people out of the country.
But Sweden is not a signatory to the UK’s Withdrawal Agreement from the EU: the presidents of the European Commission and the European Council signed on Sweden’s behalf. According to the agreement, the Commission is responsible for enforcing the agreement on member states.
The European Commission told The Local in 2024 that it is “not for the Commission” to tell Member States how strict or lenient they should be when processing late applications.
This is a pathetic response: Brits living in Sweden during Britain’s EU membership were exercising their rights as EU citizens. The EU promised them that they would be able to stay. Sweden is betraying that promise – but not lifting a finger to help, the EU is party to that betrayal. If the European Commission places any value at all on the free movement of people, it must act before more people have their lives uprooted.

items.title: Germany opens drone research centre as security threats mount
items.summary: Germany on Tuesday opened a new drone defence research centre to help combat the growing threat posed by unmanned aerial vehicles after a surge in suspicious sightings over critical infrastructure.
items.body_text:
The inauguration of the site, at a Soviet-era airfield in the former East Germany, comes less than two weeks after an explosives-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport, a key logistics hub for weapons sent to Ukraine.
Drone sightings have multiplied over other key sites, from military bases to airports, with suspicion often falling on Russia due to Germany's long-running support for Ukraine in its fight against Moscow.
Russia has consistently denied conducting any such operations.
"We are significantly strengthening our ability to respond to hostile drones," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said at the opening of the centre, which will focus on detecting and identifying unmanned aerial vehicles.
The site "will constitute a central element of the security architecture in the face of the hybrid threat posed by drones," he added at the site on a former commercial airport in Hecklingen about 200 kilometres (125 miles) south of Berlin.
Berlin uses the term hybrid warfare to refer to hostile actions short of unambiguous military attacks, including espionage, arson and sabotage, by or on behalf of foreign powers.
Last year nearly 1,000 suspicious drones flew over critical infrastructure in Germany, according to police.
Dobrindt warned that the explosive found at Leipzig earlier this month was no "isolated case".
"Leipzig is part of a wider picture," he said. "The threat situation has become more acute."
READ ALS: Germany holds security meeting over explosive drone amid Russia protest
'Detection measures needed'
Berlin has so far refused to speculate on the motives or identity of those responsible for the incident at Leipzig.
Flights to the airport were diverted for several hours as police deployed a bomb-disposal robot to remove the explosives' detonator.
The airport in eastern Germany plays a key role in the transport of military goods by the German armed forces and NATO allies. It also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.
Anke Kaysser-Pyzalla, head of the German Aerospace Centre research agency, told AFP that the new centre would focus on drone detection.
Once a drone was detected it was necessary to know "whether it was equipped with a camera or an explosive", she said.
The overall goal was "to test anti-drone defence systems under real-world conditions", she added.
About 65 people will work at the complex.
Daniel Niesler of the pilots' union Vereinigung Cockpit said Germany had to boost its detection capabilities.
"Before taking defensive measures, there are detection measures. And currently, they are not in place," he said.

items.title: German defence startup CEO in hiding after Russian plot
items.summary: The head of a German defence startup supplying attack drones to Ukraine has been living in hiding for months due to an alleged Russian assassination plot, reports said Tuesday.
items.body_text:
Donaustahl chief Stefan Thumann told broadcaster RTL and magazine Stern in a joint interview that German officials warned him in late 2025 of the plan by Russian intelligence.
The CEO -- whose company makes products including attack and reconnaissance drones, as well as military drone software -- said he has since been effectively living underground.
"I'm fighting a duel with the Russian military intelligence service for my life," he said.
"Constantly changing locations, 24-hour personal security, my private life has ceased to exist," he added.
Prosecutors announced in March the arrest of two so-called "disposable agents" -- often recruited for relatively small sums and given little training -- who allegedly spied on the CEO to prepare the assassination bid.
But the danger against him may not be over, the reports said. RTL cited a German lawmaker who said the plans targeting him were well advanced, and involved using a nerve agent.
The 39-year-old said after the "shock" of learning about the plot, he drew up his will and filled out an organ donor card.
"Things you normally don't really have on your radar at my age," he said.
He sleeps next to his computer and starts working as soon as he wakes up, to avoid dwelling on his personal situation.
The war in Ukraine has become his "very own personal war," he added.
Donaustahl is among a crop of defence tech startups in Germany who have risen to prominence by developing high-tech drones that are increasingly central to the Ukraine conflict.
In 2024, the United States foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of German defence giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, according to a CNN report.
Rheinmetall is Germany's biggest defence group and a major supplier of ammunition and weaponry to Ukraine.

items.title: Today in Germany: A roundup of the latest news on Wednesday
items.summary: Germany extends border controls until at least March of next year, new drone research centre opens following recent attacks, justice ministry campaigns for law changes to empower AC installation and more news on Wednesday, August 19th.
items.body_text:
Wednesday's top story: Germany to extend its border controls again
The controls at the German external borders are to be extended by another six months until mid-March.
Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) officially registered this with the EU Commission, a ministry spokeswoman confirmed to DPA.
"The developments at Europe's external borders show that the push back of illegal migration still needs controls," Dobrindt told the Bild newspaper.
The CSU politician had already announced the step at the end of July, when tens of thousands of migrants crossed the border from Morocco to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa. Almost all of them immediately returned to Morocco.
The borders within the EU are supposed to be open, but controls have now been carried out at all German external borders since September 16th, 2024.
Germany opens new drone research centre as security threats mount
Germany on Tuesday opened a new drone defence research centre to help combat the growing threat posed by unmanned aerial vehicles after a surge in suspicious sightings over critical infrastructure.
The inauguration of the site, at a Soviet-era airfield in the former East Germany, comes less than two weeks after an explosives-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport, a key logistics hub for weapons sent to Ukraine.

Dobrindt warned that the explosive found at Leipzig earlier this month was no "isolated case".

Federal justice ministry wants to make installing AC easier for tenants
Federal Minister of Justice Stefanie Hubig (SPD) is discussing changes to the law to make it easier for tenants to install air conditioning (AC) and sun visors.
So far, tenants in Germany have no legal right to install permanent AC systems or external shading. The landlord's consent is usually required for permanent structural changes to a property.
"Classic legal policy" could also make a contribution to heat protection, Hubig told the Rheinische Post. "I am thinking in particular of tenancy law..."
She added, however, that when structural changes are required the law would need to have some "clear and practicable regulations for both sides".
The Minister of Justice also spoke out in favour of anchoring climate adaptation as a joint task in the Basic Law: "Better protection against the consequences of climate change must become a priority issue for politics overall."
Recently, the SPD has begun pushing an amendment which would require the federal government to support states and cities with climate adaptation projects. So far heat action plans and climate preparedness has been a task for regional authorities.
Union leaders have voiced scepticism, mainly around budget concerns.
